qs.q: The Quiz page shows four buildings arranged in two rows and two columns. Each cell holds a picture, a bold title, and a caption, and everything must stay inside one page. Which HTML element is the most suitable for building this layout?

c.x: `<table>`
`<frameset>`
`<select>`
`<textarea>`

qs.e: A table arranges content in rows (``) and cells (``), and each cell can hold an image, bold text, and a caption. Four cells in two rows give the required 2 × 2 grid in a single page, whereas `` splits the window into separate pages.

qs.q: Which statement about the `<form>` element is correct?

c.x: It can contain only form controls, so paragraphs and headings are not allowed
It can contain paragraphs and headings, and also other nested `<form>` elements
It can contain paragraphs and headings, but not another `<form>` element
It can contain frames and framesets, but not text boxes or buttons

qs.e: A `<form>` is a combination of form controls (text boxes, select boxes, checkboxes, radio buttons, buttons), and it can also contain other markup such as paragraphs and headings. It must <u>not</u> contain another `<form>` element.

qs.q: Which option correctly describes the `action` and `onsubmit` attributes of the `<form>` element?

c.x: `action` selects the HTTP method to use; `onsubmit` gives the form a unique identifier
`action` is the URL of the page that handles requests; `onsubmit` runs code before sending
`action` runs code before the data is sent; `onsubmit` is the URL of the page that handles requests
`action` gives the form a unique identifier; `onsubmit` selects the HTTP method to use

qs.e: The value of `action` is the URL of the page on the Web server that handles the request. The `onsubmit` attribute provides something to run <u>before</u> the data is sent, to ensure the quality and accuracy of the submitted data. The HTTP method is set by `method`, and the unique identifier by `id`/`name`.

qs.q: A login form is submitted and the address bar shows: ``` www.example.com/login.asp?txtUsername=ahmed+&pwdPassword=123456 ``` Which method was used, and what does this show?

c.x: `get` — the form data is appended to the URL, so the password is visible
`post` — the form data is appended to the URL, so the password is visible
`get` — the form data is sent hidden from the URL, so the password is protected
`post` — the form data is sent hidden from the URL, so the password is protected

qs.e: With `method="get"` the browser appends the form data to the URL, so every value (including the password) appears in the address bar. With `method="post"` the data is not shown in the URL, which stays just `www.example.com/login.asp`.

qs.q: Study the code: ```html ``` Which attribute makes the text Search for appear inside the box when the page first loads?

c.x: `name`
`value`
`size`
`maxlength`

qs.e: The `value` attribute sets the initial content of the text box. `name` identifies the control when the data is sent, `size` sets the visible width (20), and `maxlength` limits the number of characters (64).

qs.q: In the login form, the user types a password and the box shows `●●●●●●●●`. Which input type produces this behavior?

c.x: `text`
`reset`
`password`
`image`

qs.e: `type="password"` masks the typed characters with dots, whereas `type="text"` would display them as plain text. `reset` and `image` are button-like controls, not text-entry boxes.

qs.q:
A form contains these three controls:
```html
<input type="submit" value="Submit" />
<input type="reset" value="Clear form" />
<input type="button" value="Calculate" onclick="calculate()" />
```
Which description of their behavior is correct?

c.x: Submit empties the fields, Clear form sends the data, Calculate runs `calculate()` when clicked
Submit sends the data, Clear form runs `calculate()`, Calculate empties the fields when clicked
Submit runs `calculate()`, Clear form sends the data, Calculate empties the fields when clicked
Submit sends the data, Clear form empties the fields, Calculate runs `calculate()` when clicked

qs.e: `type="submit"` sends the form data to the server, `type="reset"` clears the form back to its initial state, and `type="button"` does nothing by itself — here its `onclick` event handler runs the `calculate()` function.

qs.q: A form asks: Which of the following skills do you possess? Select all that apply. (HTML, XHTML, CSS, JavaScript, ASP, PHP). Which control type fits this question?

c.x: `radio`
`password`
`checkbox`
`reset`

qs.e: Checkboxes are used when there are multiple selections at a time, as in this example. Radio buttons are used when only one selection is needed.

qs.q:
In the flight-booking form, three radio buttons share the same name:
```html
<input type="radio" name="radClass" value="First" /> First class
<input type="radio" name="radClass" value="Business" /> Business class
<input type="radio" name="radClass" value="Economy" /> Economy class
```
What is the effect of this?

c.x: The visitor can select several classes at the same time, and all selected values are sent
The visitor can select only one class, and its value is the one sent with `radClass`
The visitor must select all three classes before the form can be submitted
The visitor can select one class, but the browser sends all three values anyway

qs.e: Radio buttons are used when only <u>one</u> selection is needed. Because they share the same `name`, they form one group: choosing one deselects the others, and only the chosen value (for example `Business`) is sent.

qs.q:
Given the code below, what does the attribute `size="6"` do?
```html
<select size="6" name="selDay">
  <option value="Mon">Monday</option>
  <option value="Tue">Tuesday</option>
  <!-- ... up to Sunday (7 options) -->
</select>
```

c.x: It limits the visitor to choosing at most six options
It makes each option name six characters long
It displays six options at a time in the list box
It starts the list from the sixth option, Saturday

qs.e: `size` sets the number of visible rows of the list box. With seven options and `size="6"`, six days (Monday to Saturday) are visible at once, and the remaining option is reached by scrolling.

qs.q: A feedback form needs a Comments box that is several lines tall and whose size is set with `rows` and `cols`. Which element should be used?

c.x: `<textarea>`
`<input type="text">`
`<select>`
`<button>`

qs.e: `<textarea name="" rows="" cols="">` creates a multi-line text box, and `rows` and `cols` set its height and width. A text-type `<input>` is only a single-line box.

qs.q: Three controls have these tab orders: `A` has `tabindex="3"`, `B` has `tabindex="1"`, and `C` has `tabindex="2"`. In which order do they receive focus when the user presses <kbd>Tab</kbd> repeatedly?

c.x: A, then B, then C
A, then C, then B
C, then B, then A
B, then C, then A

e: The `tabindex` attribute controls the order in which elements gain focus.
Pressing <kbd>Tab</kbd> moves the focus to the element with the next highest tabbing order.
Sorting by value: B (1), C (2), A (3).
<mark>Focus order: B, then C, then A</mark> (and <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> moves the focus in reverse order).

qs.q:
What does the following code create?
```html
<frameset rows="150, *, 200">
  <frame src="form4.html" />
  <frame src="form5.html" />
  <frame src="form6.html" />
</frameset>
```

c.x: Three columns: the left is 150, the right is 200, and the middle fills the rest
Three rows: the top is 150, the bottom is 200, and the middle fills the rest
Three rows of equal height, because the sizes are ignored when `*` is used
Two rows of 150 and 200, and the third page is hidden from the visitor

qs.e: `rows` splits the window horizontally, so each value describes one row. `150` and `200` are fixed sizes, and `*` takes all the remaining space. Each `<frame>` loads a separate page into its row.

qs.q:
Study the nested frameset:
```html
<frameset rows="30%, 40%, *">
  <frame src="form1.html" />
  <frameset cols="*, 400, *">
    <frame src="form2.html" />
    <frame src="form3.html" />
    <frame src="form4.html" />
  </frameset>
  <frame src="form5.html" />
</frameset>
```
How many panes does the browser window show, and how are they arranged?

c.x: Five panes: three side by side in the top row, then one in the middle row and one at the bottom
Five panes: all arranged one under another in a single column of five rows
Five panes: one on top, three side by side in the middle row, and one at the bottom
Three panes: one on top, one in the middle, and one at the bottom

e: The outer `<frameset rows=...>` divides the window into three rows (30%, 40%, and the rest).
The first row holds `form1.html` and the third row holds `form5.html`.
The second row holds an inner `<frameset cols=...>`, which splits that row into three columns.
<mark>Total: 5 panes — 1 on top, 3 side by side in the middle, 1 at the bottom.</mark>
Nesting is needed because one `<frameset>` works with either `rows` or `cols`, not both together.

qs.q: A frame must display a page from a different website, not only pages of the current site (Linked Frames). Which tag is used to create the link?

c.x: The anchor tag `<a>` with the `href` attribute
The link tag `<link>` with the `rel` attribute
The image tag `` with the `src` attribute
The form tag `<form>` with the `action` attribute

qs.e: In linked frames, the anchor tag with `href` (`<a href="...">`) is used to link the page, as in the navigation frame containing the links Wrox Press, Google, Microsoft, and BBC News.

qs.q: In the rule `h2 { font-style : italic }`, what do `h2` and `font-style` represent respectively?

c.x: Declaration and property
Selector and property
Selector and value
Property and value

qs.e: A CSS rule has two parts: a selector (what to modify, here `h2`) and a declaration (how to modify it, here `font-style : italic`). The declaration itself has a property (`font-style`) and a value (`italic`).

qs.q: Which rule applies the same color to <u>both</u> `h1` and `h2` headings?

c.x: `h1 h2 { color: blue }`
`h1; h2 { color: blue }`
`h1 . h2 { color: blue }`
`h1, h2 { color: blue }`

qs.e: A comma separates the elements to which one rule applies, so `h1, h2 { color: blue }` styles both headings. A space (`h1 h2`) creates a contextual selector instead, and a semicolon separates properties, not selectors.

qs.q: Which option correctly matches each way of adding CSS with the part of the site it affects?

c.x: Inline: all documents; Embedded: only one element; External: only the document it appears in
Inline: only the document it appears in; Embedded: all linked documents; External: only one element
Inline: only one element; Embedded: only the document it appears in; External: all documents linked to it
Inline: only one element; Embedded: all linked documents; External: only the document it appears in

qs.e: Inline styles are written in the line where the style is needed and affect only that element. Embedded styles sit in the `` of the page and affect only that document. External (linked) style sheets affect every document they are attached to.

qs.q: Where is an embedded (internal) style sheet written, and with which tags?

c.x: In the `<head>` section, between `<style>` and `</style>`
In the `<head>` section, between `<link>` and `</link>`
In the `<body>` section, between `<script>` and `</script>`
In the `<head>` section, between `<css>` and `</css>`

qs.e: Embedded style rules are grouped with the `<STYLE> ... </STYLE>` tag pair inside the `<head>` of the HTML page. `<link>` is used to reference an external file instead, and `<script>` is for JavaScript.

qs.q: Which is the correct way to give the whole page a yellow background using an inline style?

c.x: `<body style="background-color=yellow">`
`<body style="background-color:yellow">`
`<body style="color-background:yellow">`
`<body class="background-color:yellow">`

qs.e: The inline syntax is `<TAG STYLE="PROPERTY : VALUE">`. A colon (not `=`) separates the property `background-color` from its value, and the attribute must be `style`, not `class`.

c.x: Arial font, bold text only, red text color, size 18pt
Italic and bold text, red text color, size 18pt, in the default font
Arial font, italic and bold text, red background, size 18pt
Arial font, italic and bold text, red text color, size 18pt

qs.e: Each declaration sets one property: `font-family` gives Arial, `font-style` gives italic, `font-weight` gives bold, `color` gives red <u>text</u>, and `font-size` gives 18pt. Changing the background would need `background-color`.

qs.q: Which rule makes the text of <u>all</u> paragraphs bold?

c.x: `p { font-style: bold; }`
`p { text-weight: bold; }`
`p { font-weight: bold; }`
`.p { font-weight: bold; }`

qs.e:
`font-weight` controls how thick the text is, so `p { font-weight: bold; }` styles every paragraph. `font-style` is for italic or normal style, `text-weight` is not a CSS property, and `.p` would select elements with class `p` instead of `

` elements.

qs.q: Which rule makes the text of all paragraphs red on a yellow background?

c.x: `p { color: red; background-color: yellow; }`
`p { color: yellow; background-color: red; }`
`p { color: red, background-color: yellow; }`
`p { color: red: background-color: yellow; }`

qs.e: `color` sets the text color and `background-color` sets the color behind it. Declarations are separated by a <u>semicolon</u>, not by a comma or a colon, so only the first option is correct.

qs.q: A designer wants to change <u>only</u> the color of an element's border. Which property should be used?

c.x: `border-style`
`border-color`
`border-width`
`margin`

qs.e: The Border properties are `border-style`, `border-width`, and `border-color`; the last one sets the color. `margin` is a different box property that controls the space outside the border.

qs.q: Which property from the Text Properties group is used to change the capitalization of text, for example to make the first letter of every word a capital letter?

c.x: `text-indent`
`text-align`
`letter-spacing`
`text-transform`

qs.e: `text-transform` controls the case of text; for example `text-transform: capitalize` makes the first letter of each word a capital letter. `text-indent` indents the first line, `text-align` aligns the text, and `letter-spacing` changes the space between characters.

qs.q: Which option correctly describes the selector used to style <u>one unique</u> element?

c.x: A class selector, written with `#` and matched to the `class` attribute
A class selector, written with `.` and matched to the `id` attribute
An ID selector, written with `#` and matched to the `id` attribute
An ID selector, written with `.` and matched to the `id` attribute

qs.e: ID selectors start with the hash symbol `#` and match the element's `id` attribute, which names a single element uniquely. Class selectors start with a dot `.` and match the `class` attribute.

qs.q:
Given the code below, which description of the rendered page is correct? ```html

Mansoura University

Default

Faculty of Computer & Information Sciences

```

c.x: The first heading is red, the second keeps the default color, and the third is blue
The first heading is blue, the second keeps the default color, and the third is red
The first and second headings are red, and the third is blue
The first heading is red, and the second and third headings are blue

e: `#syntax` matches the element with `id="syntax"`, so the first `<h1>` is red.
The second `<h1>` has no `id`, so no rule matches it and it keeps the default style.
`#note` matches the `<h2>` with `id="note"`, so it is blue.

qs.q:
Given the code below, which statement is correct? ```html

Mansoura University

Default

Faculty of Computer & Information Sciences

```

c.x: `.note` styles the `<h2>` through its id, and `#syntax` styles the first `<h1>` through its class
`.note` styles the `<h2>` through its class, and `#syntax` styles the first `<h1>` through its id
`.note` styles the first `<h1>` through its id, and `#syntax` styles the `<h2>` through its class
`.note` styles every heading, and `#syntax` styles only the second `<h1>`

qs.e: Class selectors (`.note`) match elements by their `class` attribute, and ID selectors (`#syntax`) match by `id`. Here the `<h2 class="note">` is blue, the `<h1 id="syntax">` is red, and the plain `<h1>` stays in the default style.

qs.q:
In this page, why does the ordered list appear magenta while the unordered list appears white? ```html
  • Apples
  • Bananas
  1. Apples
  2. Bananas
```

c.x: `UL` inherits the color of `Body`, while the `OL` rule overrides the inherited color
Both lists inherit the color of `Body`, and the `UL` rule is ignored
Neither list inherits from `Body`, because each list needs its own color rule
`OL` inherits the color of `Body`, while the `UL` rule overrides the inherited color

qs.e: Elements inside `<body>` inherit its style by default, so the `<ol>` (which has no rule of its own) is magenta. Since the unordered list needs a different setting, the `UL` rule overrides the inherited color and makes it white.

qs.q: Which option correctly connects an external style sheet 1.css to an HTML page?

c.x: `<style rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" src="1.css"/>` inside `<head>`
`<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" src="1.css"/>` inside `<head>`
`<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="1.css"/>` inside `<head>`
`<script rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="1.css"/>` inside `<head>`

qs.e: An external CSS file is referenced with `<link>` in the `<head>` of each HTML page, using `rel="stylesheet"`, `type="text/css"` and `href="1.css"`. `<style>` is for embedded rules, `<script>` is for JavaScript, and the file name goes in `href`, not `src`.
